title: GPU bisect: kernel choice, on-prem/VPC quantization & batching proofing
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Northbridge through a targeted bisect plan to isolate a kernel-path instability observed on customer on-prem A100 fleet. Discussion covered TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM behavior under CUDA graph replay, how KV cache priming and batching amplify nondeterminism, and practical quantization tradeoffs for latency-sensitive pipelines. Agreed next steps: run microbench harness, share trace/benchmark templates, and schedule follow-up to review bisect results.
action_items: Maya Chen: Share benchmark template, example CUDA graph trace file, and upload link (due: 2025-08-08)
Arjun Patel: Send kernel selection checklist and Nsight/Perf steps for collecting per-launch kernel timings (due: 2025-08-12)
Liam O'Connor: Run the microbench on on-prem 4xA100 node with controlled prompt set and upload traces to shared S3 (due: 2025-08-15)
next_steps: Schedule 45m follow-up to review bisect results and decide pilot (Maya to propose windows)
If bisect indicates TensorRT-LLM path is stable, start 2-week pilot on Redwood Dedicated (customer to confirm procurement path)
Confirm security contact and provide VPC onboarding checklist
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-08-05 14:30 PT | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Arjun (Redwood SE), Liam (Northbridge ML), Sofia (Infra), David (Platform)

SUMMARY: Quick technical deep dive to triage kernel path instability on customer's on-prem A100 cluster. Goal is to produce a reproducible bisect and decide whether TRT-LLM or vLLM path is preferred for their low-latency inference.

TOPICS: kernel selection; cuda graph replay instability; kv cache priming effects; batching latency vs throughput; quantization precision vs stability; VPC/on-prem constraints.

[00:00] Maya: Hey thanks everyone for taking the time, we'll keep this focused — two goals, one to see what data you already have around the nondeterministic slowdowns, and two, propose a bisect plan that we can run on your on-prem cluster.
[00:18] Liam: Yeah thanks, appreciate it. We've been seeing intermittent 200-400ms tail spikes on our 1k token conversational workload, more common after a longer context. It seems to line up with CUDA graph replay, or when the KV is hot, but not entirely sure.
[00:34] Arjun: Right, that matches a couple of kernels we've seen flip between cuBLAS gemm variants and a specialized fused attention kernel — sometimes TRT-LLM picks a different execution path.
[00:48] Sofia: Quick clarification — our infra is a 4xA100 NVLink chassis on-prem, Ubuntu 20.04 with driver 525, and we run inside our VPC-like network but air-gapped except for s3 egress.
[01:05] David: Also we have quantized some weights to int8 for batch inference for some endpoints to save cost. Not all models are quantized though.
[01:12] Maya: Great, that helps. So two axes: model execution path (TRT-LLM vs vLLM), and runtime heuristics (cuda graph replay + kernel selection). For the bisect we'll try to control batching, KV priming, and quantization on/off.
[01:30] Liam: When you say KV priming, are you referring to warmstart primer tokens vs persistent kv cache population? We do both, and we've observed worse behavior when the cache is warmed across many sessions.
[01:44] Arjun: Yes exactly. Persistent KV cache across requests changes the memory access pattern; it can change kernel selection heuristics and increase register pressure, which can cause a kernel switch that has a slower path or more memory thrash.
[02:00] Maya: Also worth noting that CUDA graph replay can hide per-launch variability but replaying the wrong shape/launch pattern can repeat a bad path. So we want to capture an NVTX trace and a small cudagraph replay log to see if the graph snapshot aligns to the slow step.
[02:18] Liam: Sounds good — we can attach nvprof or Nsight traces. We tried nvprof but our ops names are obfuscated in the TRT-LLM layer sometimes, so we need the mapping.
[02:30] Arjun: We'll share a small script that collects per-kernel times and maps TRT kernels back to the model ops — it uses Nsight and the TRT-LLM symbol map we generate during model build.
[02:40] Sofia: Is there any known issue with driver 525? We considered bumping to 530 but that requires more validation.
[02:48] Arjun: There's a couple of patched regressions in the 530 branch around nvlink scheduling, but upgrading kernel/driver has its own risk. For the bisect we prefer to bisect the runtime path first at your current driver level.
[03:02] David: For quantization, when we flip int8 off we saw a small latency increase nominally but sometimes the tail spikes decreased — maybe because quantized kernels pick a different fallback path?
[03:15] Arjun: Correct. Int8 routes can force different GEMM backends or calibration paths — sometimes those backends are less mature and have less robust fallback heuristics leading to more edge-case slowdowns.
[03:28] Maya: So plan: 1) baseline microbench with 1-beam single-token latency, 2) run longer context runs (1k tokens) with KV warm and cold, 3) run with quantized and fp16, 4) collect Nsight/NVTX traces and cudagraph snapshots, 5) run TRT-LLM and vLLM variants and compare kernel histograms.
[03:50] Liam: That sounds right. How intrusive is the Nsight capture? We can't have production traffic impacted.
[03:57] Arjun: We'll provide a lightweight perf harness that runs on a shadow node with the same image; Nsight sampling mode is low overhead and you can throttle frequency. For full launch times we recommend a short dedicated run.
[04:12] Sofia: Okay. Curious — is Redwood's runtime doing any kernel remapping at runtime? We've seen some vendor runtimes rewrite kernels.
[04:22] Maya: Redwood's runtime selects kernels based on heuristics (sequence length, batch size, kv size) and will prefer quantized kernels when configured. There's also a kernel selection table we can export for a given model build to see the chosen path.
[04:36] Arjun: And we have a fallback policy: if TRT-LLM path fails a health check we can swap to vLLM compatible path automatically, but that swap itself can promote a brief spike while caches are repopulated.
[04:49] Liam: That automatic swap did happen once during a weekend run and caused a 1s spike. Not great.
[04:55] Maya: Understood. That's why the bisect objective is twofold: identify the root kernel(s) that flip and then test whether changing runtime knobs (disable cuda-graph replay, tweak batch sizing, or switch quantization profile) reduces occurrence.
[05:10] David: We have a sample prompt deck and a synthetic traffic generator. We'll run whatever harness you give.
[05:16] Arjun: Excellent. A couple of gotchas to call out: 1) cudagraphs captured with variable shapes will replay incorrectly — so ensure your capture shape set matches real long-context shapes; 2) persistent kv priming across sessions can make per-request memory map different; 3) small batch widths can cause repeated kernel selection churn — try both microbatch=1 and microbatch=8.
[05:40] Maya: We'll also include a tiny test to force kernel switch by toggling sequence length mid-run to see if the scheduler flips to a different GEMM.
[05:50] Liam: If the bisect points us at TRT fused attention as the culprit, what are our options? Patch, fallback, or change model build?
[05:58] Arjun: Patching fused kernels is possible but slow; immediate options are: a) prefer vLLM path for that model on that cluster, b) adjust batch/sequence length to avoid the pathological region, or c) tweak quantization profile to use a more stable GEMM backend.
[06:12] Sofia: What about memory fragmentation and eviction — could that present like a kernel slowness?
[06:17] Arjun: Yes, fragmentation and L2 thrash can change occupancy. We'll capture GPU-memory allocation strat to see if large allocations coincide with slow calls.
[06:25] Maya: I'll share a short checklist for what logs to collect and how to anonymize PII in traces. Also we'll provide a shared S3 bucket link for uploads — we've done this before for air-gapped customers using a jump host.
[06:38] Liam: Perfect. Any known interactions with VPCs? We don't expect network to be the cause but our KV store is in a private NFS that mounts; could that latency influence the runtime?
[06:49] Arjun: If KV is stored off-GPU and the runtime fetches synchronously, yes. Redwood's preferred pattern is in-GPU KV or prefetching stages. We'll include a test to measure end-to-end fetch times separate from kernel times.
[07:04] David: Ok quick question on benchmarks: What metrics should we capture beyond p50/p95/p99?
[07:10] Arjun: Also capture kernel-level percentiles, GPU occupancy, memory allocation events, and cudagraph replay times. A CSV with per-request token timings plus an annotated NVTX timeline is ideal.
[07:22] Sofia: We'll try to get the traces by next week. Anything else to watch for?
[07:28] Maya: One more: be cautious with thrash from other tenants on the chassis if you share nodes. Try to isolate the test node.
[07:36] Liam: We're good to isolate.
[07:40] Arjun: I'll also include a short script that toggles quantization on the fly to reproduce the int8->fp16 behavior. That helped other customers pinpoint a bad GEMM implementation.
[07:52] Maya: Ok let's recap action items — (recap briefly).
[08:00] Liam: Quick note — our security team will need the VPC checklist before we talk about pilot procurement.
[08:05] Maya: We'll include that in the shared folder.
[08:09] Sofia: Great, thanks everyone.
[08:12] Maya: Thanks all — we'll send the template and NVTX capture instructions shortly and propose a follow-up slot.

NOTES: Transcript contains occasional filler and automatic speaker-label errors from live transcription. We included timestamps at ~regular intervals.
